title: Dating a surface you can’t visit
teaches: How counting craters gives an age, and how the Apollo and Luna samples turned the count into years

blocks.text: Look at the full Moon and you see two kinds of ground. The dark patches, which early observers took for seas and named **maria** (singular *mare*, Latin for sea), are smooth plains. The bright ground between them, the **highlands**, is rougher and higher. Through a telescope the difference is obvious in another way: the highlands are covered in craters, overlapping one another until there is hardly any flat ground left, while the maria have only a scattering.

blocks.caption: The full Moon. The dark maria are plains of basalt lava; the bright highlands are older crust, crowded with craters.

blocks.text: That difference is a clock of a kind. Rocks fall on the Moon all the time, and with no air, no water and no moving plates to wipe the record, every crater stays until another impact destroys it. A surface that has been exposed for longer has collected more craters. So the maria, with fewer craters, are younger than the highlands, which agrees with what the eye shows directly: in many places the dark lava has flowed into old craters and basins and filled them, which only a later flow could do. This is lesson 1's principle of superposition, applied from a quarter of a million miles away.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The maria are dark, smooth lava plains; the highlands are bright, rough and densely cratered.
With no erosion, craters accumulate, so a surface with more craters has been exposed for longer.
Crater counts give relative ages: the maria are younger than the highlands.

blocks.text: Counting craters is careful work. Geologists choose a patch of a single surface, such as one lava plain, measure every crater on it above a certain size, and divide by the area to get a density, usually the number of craters wider than 1 kilometre per square kilometre. Small craters vastly outnumber large ones (for each crater 10 km across there are roughly a hundred 1 km across), so even a small area gives a usable count.

There are traps. A large impact throws out debris that lands nearby and makes clusters and chains of smaller **secondary craters**, which are not independent arrivals from space and must be left out. On a very old surface, craters are so crowded that every new one destroys old ones: the surface is **saturated**, and its count stops rising however much older it gets. The Moon's highlands are close to that state, which is why the true age of the oldest highland surfaces cannot be read from counts alone.

Before Apollo, counts could rank lunar surfaces from older to younger, and the USGS geologists of lesson P1, Eugene Shoemaker and Robert Hackman among them, used them, together with which deposit lay on which, to draw the first geological maps of the Moon. What counts could not do was say how many years each surface had been exposed. That needed the rate at which craters form, and nobody knew whether it had been steady. Estimates for the age of the maria ranged from a few hundred million to several billion years.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A crater count is the number of craters above a size, per unit area, on one surface.
Secondary craters from nearby impacts must be excluded, and very old surfaces become saturated.
Counts alone rank surfaces by age but cannot give years without knowing the impact rate.

blocks.text: Apollo supplied the missing piece. Each crew landed on a surface whose craters had already been counted from orbital photographs, and brought back rocks that could be dated with the radioactive clocks of lesson 7. The Soviet Union's robotic Luna 16, 20 and 24 missions, between 1970 and 1976, returned a further 300 grams or so of soil from three more sites.

The mare basalts turned out to be old: 3.6 to 3.8 billion years at Apollo 11's Sea of Tranquility, 3.75 billion at Apollo 17, 3.3 billion at Apollo 15 and Luna 24, about 3.15 billion at Apollo 12's Ocean of Storms. Highland rocks gave older ages, around 3.9 billion years for most, with fragments of the first crust older still. Some samples dated individual craters. Material that Apollo 12 picked up from a bright ray of debris crossing its landing site gave an age of about 800 million years for the crater Copernicus, which threw it out; a landslide at Apollo 17, triggered by debris from the crater Tycho, gave Tycho about 100 million years.

blocks.caption: Apollo 12's Pete Conrad beside Surveyor 3, a robotic lander that had sat on the Moon for two and a half years. The crew landed within walking distance and brought pieces of it home.

blocks.text: Put a count and an age together for each site and the impact rate appears, and it was not steady. On the young surfaces, Copernicus and Tycho and the mare plains younger than about 3 billion years, the count grows in proportion to age: craters have arrived at a roughly constant rate for the last 3 billion years. But a surface 3.8 billion years old has far more craters than a steady rate would give it. Before about 3.8 billion years ago, impacts were hundreds of times more frequent than they are now, the tail of the bombardment by debris left over from the building of the planets.

blocks.caption: Left, a patch of the Moon 50 km on a side, with every crater over 1 km that it would have collected by the age you set. Right, crater density against age (on a scale where each step up is ten times the last), from a curve fitted to the dated samples by Gerhard Neukum (2001); gold dots mark the samples.
blocks.task: Date the mystery plain from its count

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Apollo and Luna samples gave radiometric ages to surfaces whose craters had been counted.
Mare basalts are about 3.1 to 3.8 billion years old; most highland rocks are older still.
For the last 3 billion years craters have formed at a roughly steady rate; before about 3.8 billion years ago the rate was far higher.

blocks.text: One feature of the dates puzzled the people who measured them. In 1974 Fouad Tera, Dimitri Papanastassiou and Gerald Wasserburg at Caltech noticed that rocks melted by impacts, from all the Apollo highland sites, gave ages clustered around 3.9 billion years, with few older. They proposed a **lunar cataclysm**: a short spike of heavy bombardment long after the planets formed, perhaps when the orbits of the giant planets shifted and scattered asteroids inward. Others argued that the clustering came from where the samples were collected: the great Imbrium basin, about 3.9 billion years old, threw debris across much of the near side, where every Apollo crew landed.

The question is still open, and it is a good example of how a dating method carries its sampling with it. Meteorites knocked off the Moon and found in Antarctica and the Sahara come from random places on its surface, including the far side, and many of them show older impact melts, which weakens the case for a single storm. Rocks from the Chinese Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6 missions (2020 and 2024), the first fresh samples in nearly fifty years, are now filling gaps in the curve.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Many Apollo impact-melt rocks date to about 3.9 billion years, which led to the idea of a short late cataclysm.
The clustering may instead reflect debris from one basin, Imbrium, spread across the Apollo sites; the debate continues.

blocks.text: The Moon is the only body for which crater counts have been calibrated with rocks from known places, and that makes it the reference for the rest of the solar system. To date a lava plain on Mars or Mercury, planetary geologists count its craters and convert the count to an age using the lunar curve, adjusted for how much more often each planet is hit and how fast impacts arrive there. That is how we know that the giant Martian volcano Olympus Mons has lava flows only tens of millions of years old, and that much of Mars's southern highlands is older than 3.5 billion years.

Those ages carry larger uncertainties than lunar ones, because the corrections are estimates. The same steps apply: count, exclude secondaries, watch for saturation, and convert with a curve fixed by dated samples. Every crater age on another world rests on a few hundred kilograms of rock from six Apollo sites and three Luna sites.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The calibrated lunar curve, adjusted for each planet's impact rate, is used to date surfaces on Mars, Mercury and other bodies.
Those ages are less certain, because the adjustments are estimates rather than measurements.

blocks.caption: Six questions on crater ages
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why do craters build up on the Moon, where on Earth most of them have disappeared?
choices: The Moon has no air, water or moving plates to erase them
The Moon is hit far more often than the Earth
Lunar rock is too hard to wear away
items.why: On Earth, weather, rivers and plate tectonics destroy craters within tens or hundreds of millions of years. On the Moon a crater stays until another impact wipes it out.

items.ask: Besides having fewer craters, what else shows that the maria are younger than the highlands?
choices: Mare lava has flowed into older craters and basins and filled them
The maria are higher than the highlands
The maria are darker, and dark rock is always younger
items.why: A lava flow that fills an existing hole must be younger than the hole. It is superposition read on the Moon's surface.

items.ask: Why must secondary craters be left out of a count?
choices: They are made by debris from a nearby impact, not by separate arrivals from space
They are too small to measure
They are volcanic vents, not craters
items.why: Secondary craters cluster around large craters and are not independent hits. Counting them would make a surface look older than it is.

items.ask: A highland surface has about ten times as many craters as a 3.6-billion-year-old mare. About how old is it?
items.why: Before about 3.8 billion years ago the impact rate was far higher, so a few hundred million extra years of exposure were enough to multiply the count.

items.ask: What did the Apollo samples add that crater counts alone could not give?
choices: Ages in years for surfaces whose craters had been counted, which fixed the impact rate
The first proof that the maria are made of lava
Evidence that the impact rate has never changed
items.why: Radiometric dates from known sites turned relative crater ages into absolute ones and showed how the impact rate changed over time.

items.ask: What is shown here, and how did it help date the Moon?
choices: An Apollo 12 astronaut at an earlier robotic lander; the crew's landing site gave dated rocks for one of the counted surfaces
A Soviet rover collecting the first lunar soil
items.why: Apollo 12 landed in the Ocean of Storms beside Surveyor 3. Its basalts, about 3.15 billion years old, are one of the calibration points of the crater curve.

learned: Crater density measures how long a surface has been exposed, so counts rank surfaces by age.
Apollo and Luna samples dated counted surfaces, turning counts into years.
Impacts were far more frequent before about 3.8 billion years ago and roughly steady for the last 3 billion.
The calibrated lunar curve is used to date surfaces on Mars, Mercury and beyond.
